title: Assessing the effect of therapeutic level of oxytetracycline dihydrate on pharmacokinetics and biosafety in Oncorhynchus

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines AUC_Trapezoid = Σ(C_i + C_{i+1})·(t_{i+1} - t_i). The standard trapezoidal rule requires a factor of 1/2: AUC = Σ 0.5·(C_i + C_{i+1})·(t_{i+1} - t_i). As written, the formula is missing this coefficient, which would double every computed AUC value relative to the correct trapezoidal estimate.

The text states: 'the shortest half-life observed in the gill tissue (0.94 h), followed by the liver (5.75 h), kidney (13.12 h), skin (9.88 h), and muscle (17.23 h).' This implies an ascending order, but skin's value (9.88 h) is actually smaller than kidney's (13.12 h), so the stated sequence is internally inconsistent with the numbers given.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, Pharmacokinetic result paragraph (elimination rate constant vs half-life for gill)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The gill is reported to have the shortest half-life (0.94 h) and separately the 'highest value' of the elimination rate constant (0.01 h⁻¹). Using the paper's own formula t1/2 = ln(2)/k, a half-life of 0.94 h implies k ≈ 0.737 h⁻¹, nearly 74-fold higher than the stated 0.01 h⁻¹, making these two reported values for the same tissue mathematically incompatible.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, Pharmacokinetic result paragraph (muscle half-life values)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Muscle's half-life is first reported as 17.23 h in the general tissue half-life comparison ('...and muscle (17.23 h)'), but the same number is later reused specifically as the 'initial distribution half-life (t1/2a)' while a new 'elimination half-life (t1/2b)' of 20.56 h is introduced, without clarifying that the first-mentioned value only represented a sub-phase rather than the overall half-life.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, Pharmacokinetic result paragraph (liver half-life values)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Liver's half-life is first given as 5.75 h in the general tissue half-life list, but later the same figure is re-characterized as only the 'initial distribution half-life,' while a dramatically different 'elimination half-life' of 238.68 h (over 40-fold larger) is introduced without reconciling why the earlier statement presented 5.75 h as simply 'the half-life.'

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, Pharmacokinetic result paragraph ('duration of elimination phase')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text reports 'the longest duration [of elimination phase] was observed in the liver at 606.33 h' (~25 days), but the PK study's sampling only extended to 128 h (and the abstract states the PK study spanned only 5 days, ~120 h). No extrapolation methodology is described to justify a derived duration nearly 5x longer than the actual observation window.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods ('Preparation of medicated feed') vs Results ('Pharmacokinetic result' introduction)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The 'Preparation of medicated feed' section describes mixing oxytetracycline dihydrate into vegetable oil/feed, drying it, and storing it for voluntary feeding ('stored at a temperature of 4°C for immediate use'), implying normal oral ingestion. However, the Results section states the single dose for the PK study was administered 'through gavaging in semi liquid form,' describing a fundamentally different administration route (forced gavage of a liquid) for what should be the same 80 mg/kg single-dose experiment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods (non-compartmental pharmacokinetic model) vs Results (distribution/elimination phase half-lives)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Methods state pharmacokinetic parameters 'were assessed using a non-compartmental pharmacokinetic model grounded in statistical moment theory.' However, the Results describe distinct 'initial distribution half-life (t1/2a)' and 'elimination half-life (t1/2b)' phases for muscle and liver, a multi-exponential/compartmental concept that is inconsistent with a purely non-compartmental analytical framework.
